sections.sectionText: Every day, people make decisions about systems that touch millions of lives: how long someone waits in an emergency room, which neighborhoods get bus routes, how a platform decides what you see next. Those decisions are rarely made on instinct alone. They are made with data, whether the decision-maker knows it or not. This course is built on a simple provocation: the practice of understanding human needs and designing better systems is not just a qualitative endeavor. Done rigorously, it is one of the most demanding forms of quantitative reasoning there is. These are the same questions that drive human-centered practice across every field — except here, students learn to answer them with data. Enrollment in this course is limited to undergraduate students; graduate students are not eligible, and no exceptions will be made. Design Thinking, Systems Thinking, and AI Agents Most of us have used AI to answer a question or draft something quickly. Fewer of us have used it to run an entire process from beginning to end, the kind of work that normally takes a team: researching a market and turning it into a report, producing a weekly publication, or taking an app from an idea to the App Store. This 8-week, project-based course brings those two ideas together. Using Human-Centered Design (HCD), you will learn to understand a problem through the people who live with it, then use systems thinking to see the structure producing it, including the parts that are not obvious at first look. From there, you will design a workflow for the outcome you want and use agentic coding tools such as Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode to build a set of AI agents that produces it. You will run your system against real work, notice where it falls short, and improve the design rather than the individual result. The course moves through the HCD phases you would recognize from any design thinking course. What changes is where you land. Instead of ending at a prototype of a product, you end at a working system that produces an outcome, and you are the person who designed it. Each student proposes their own project, so the work stays tied to something you find genuinely interesting. You will work individually on your project and sit in a standing critique group that follows your work through the whole course. Human-Centered Product Management teaches students to run the full arc from human insight to a defensible product decision. Most HCD courses end at a validated prototype; most product management instruction starts from a roadmap that already exists. This course closes that gap: students use the human-centered design process — empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test — to generate insight, then apply core product management practice — opportunity sizing, prioritization frameworks, PRDs, go-to-market planning, and metrics — to turn that insight into a decision they can defend to a real stakeholder. Working in teams against a live partner project, students leave with a full-cycle artifact: research synthesis, a prioritized roadmap, a tested prototype, and a launch and measurement plan, plus practice presenting that reasoning to a non-classroom audience. DTX 251 (Introduction to Design Thinking) or equivalent HCD experience, recommended but not required. sections.sectionText: Although a Friday class meeting time is listed in the schedule, students are not expected to attend a formal class session on Fridays. This time block is intentionally reserved to support collaborative learning by ensuring that all students have a common period available in their schedules. Instructors may encourage teams to use this time for group meetings, project work, consultations, workshops, or other course-related activities as needed throughout the semester as needed. Graduate students are NOT permitted to enroll in this course under any circumstances. Graduate students should not attempt to register for this course, and no exceptions will be granted. Please do not contact the instructor or department regarding enrollment eligibility, as requests for exceptions will not be considered. If you are a graduate student interested in design-related learning opportunities, we welcome you to explore our workshops, which are available for graduate student registration here https://designcenter.illinois.edu/events/workshops.
